steps.rendered_prompt:
You are writing a short explainer script from a research record.

Audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy
Target spoken duration: about 60 seconds.

Write the script from the research record below. Make it accurate and easy to follow.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it, in exactly this shape:

{
  "case_id": "C06",
  "audience": "General public with secondary-school science literacy",
  "target_duration_s": 60,
  "beats": [
    {"beat": "short label", "narration": "what the narrator says",
     "on_screen": "what is shown", "claim_refs": []}
  ]
}

RESEARCH RECORD
---------------
A microbiome-transfer result whose key control lives in the supplement

Record
SYN-C06

Study design
Controlled preclinical transfer experiment

Background
Transfer of gut microbial communities between hosts is the standard experimental approach to testing whether a microbiota phenotype is transmissible. Germ-free recipients are used because they have no resident community to displace. Donor-to-donor variation is a recognised feature of this design, and studies differ in how many donor pairs they report.

Abstract
Faecal microbiota transfer from lean to obese donors has been proposed to improve metabolic phenotype. We transferred microbiota from lean donor mice into germ-free recipients and measured fat mass at 8 weeks. Recipients of lean-donor microbiota gained 24% less fat mass than recipients of obese-donor microbiota (p = 0.003, n = 20 per group).

Methods
Germ-free C57BL/6J recipients were colonised at 6 weeks and maintained on a standardised chow diet. Analyses in the main text use donor pair 1. Donor pairs 2-4 and the pair-fed arm are in the supplementary materials. Body composition was measured by EchoMRI at 8 weeks. Cages were changed on a fixed schedule and recipients were single-housed after colonisation. Donor communities were characterised by 16S sequencing. Food intake was recorded daily in all arms.

Results
  location: Main text; finding: Donor pair 1: lean-donor recipients gained 24% less fat mass (p = 0.003)

Supplementary materials
  S3: Across all four donor pairs the effect was inconsistent: donor pair 1, -24% (p = 0.003); donor pair 2, -6% (p = 0.41); donor pair 3, +3% (p = 0.72); donor pair 4, -19% (p = 0.04). Pooled across pairs the difference was -11% (95% CI -23% to +1%), which does not exclude no effect.
  S2: In the diet-matched control arm, in which recipients were pair-fed to equalise intake, the difference in fat mass between lean-donor and obese-donor recipients was not significant (-4%, p = 0.55), indicating that a substantial part of the main-text effect is attributable to differences in food intake rather than to the transferred microbiota.

Discussion
These data support a causal contribution of the gut microbiota to host adiposity. Colonisation with lean-donor communities produced a clear reduction in fat-mass gain in the primary comparison. The full donor-pair series and the pair-fed arm are provided as supplementary materials for readers wishing to examine heterogeneity.

Limitations
  Fat mass was the only metabolic endpoint reported in the main text.

Conclusion
Transfer of lean-donor microbiota reduced fat-mass gain in germ-free recipients in the primary donor pair.

Data availability
Sequencing data are deposited under accession SYN-C06. Supplementary Table S3 and Supplementary Figure S2 accompany this record and contain the full donor-pair series and the pair-fed arm.

final_script.audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy

beats.narration: Can the microbes in your gut change how much fat you carry? Scientists test this by transplanting gut bacteria from one mouse into another that was raised with no microbes of its own.
beats.on_screen: Simple diagram: donor mouse gut bacteria transferred into a germ-free recipient mouse

beats.narration: In this study, recipients given bacteria from a lean donor gained twenty-four percent less fat over eight weeks than those given bacteria from an obese donor. Twenty mice per group, and a convincingly small p-value.
beats.on_screen: Bar chart: lean-donor vs obese-donor fat mass, -24%, p = 0.003

beats.narration: But that headline used only one donor pair. Three more pairs sit in the supplementary materials, and they disagree: minus six percent, plus three, minus nineteen. Pool all four and the effect shrinks to about minus eleven percent, with a range that includes no effect at all.
beats.on_screen: Four donor pairs plotted side by side, then pooled estimate with confidence interval crossing zero

beats.beat: It may be the food, not the bugs
beats.narration: There is a second control in the supplement too. When the mice were fed matched amounts of food, the difference nearly vanished: four percent, not statistically significant. So much of the original effect looks like the mice simply eating different amounts.
beats.on_screen: Side-by-side: free feeding -24% vs pair-fed -4%, p = 0.55; food bowl icon

beats.narration: The paper concludes the microbiota drives fat gain. The supplement suggests a smaller, shakier story. When a result rests on one comparison and the controls are filed at the back, it is worth reading to the end.
beats.on_screen: Text card: 'One donor pair is not four. Check the supplement.'

final_narration:
Can the microbes in your gut change how much fat you carry? Scientists test this by transplanting gut bacteria from one mouse into another that was raised with no microbes of its own.
In this study, recipients given bacteria from a lean donor gained twenty-four percent less fat over eight weeks than those given bacteria from an obese donor. Twenty mice per group, and a convincingly small p-value.
But that headline used only one donor pair. Three more pairs sit in the supplementary materials, and they disagree: minus six percent, plus three, minus nineteen. Pool all four and the effect shrinks to about minus eleven percent, with a range that includes no effect at all.
There is a second control in the supplement too. When the mice were fed matched amounts of food, the difference nearly vanished: four percent, not statistically significant. So much of the original effect looks like the mice simply eating different amounts.
The paper concludes the microbiota drives fat gain. The supplement suggests a smaller, shakier story. When a result rests on one comparison and the controls are filed at the back, it is worth reading to the end.
